title: Population-level risks of alcohol consumption by amount, geography, age, sex, and year: A systematic analysis for the Global Burden of Disease Study 2020

claims.statement: In the world's population, alcohol use compared with no alcohol use is estimated by two global models to account for about 2.3 million (2004, after subtracting deaths the model counted as prevented; editors' rounding) to 2.8 million (2016) deaths a year. The Global Burden of Disease 2016 study estimated 2.8 million deaths in 2016 (95% uncertainty interval 2.4–3.3 million), 2.2% of age-standardised deaths in women and 6.8% in men, about 2 and 7 in every 100; it ranked alcohol seventh among risk factors overall and first at ages 15 to 49, where 3.8% of women's and 12.2% of men's deaths were attributed to it, the leading causes being tuberculosis, road injuries and self-harm (Griswold et al., 2018; funded by the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation). A WHO comparative risk assessment for 2004 estimated 2482 thousand deaths caused by alcohol, less 227 thousand deaths it modelled as prevented (215 thousand from heart and blood-vessel disease, 12 thousand from diabetes), leaving 2255 thousand, 3.8 in every 100 deaths worldwide (6.3 in 100 deaths of men and 1.1 in 100 of women) and 5.3 in 100 deaths before the age of 60; the deaths caused were mainly from unintentional injuries (666 thousand), heart and blood-vessel disease (545 thousand), cancer (487 thousand), liver cirrhosis (373 thousand) and intentional injuries (272 thousand) (Rehm et al., 2009; the underlying assessments supported by WHO and the Swiss Federal Office of Public Health; no conflicts declared). These are model estimates, not counted deaths: they combine estimated drinking (sales data, estimates of unrecorded alcohol, which is more than a quarter of the world's drinking, and surveys) with relative-risk curves from observational studies, mostly of middle-class cohorts in high-income countries, applied to every population. The 2004 estimate has no uncertainty intervals, and the 2016 paper does not say that its intervals include uncertainty from the model's structure or from bias in the underlying studies; the net figures depend on protective heart and diabetes estimates at low intake, which the 2004 authors call controversial; the 2016 figure is counted against a minimum-risk level of zero drinks a day, whose interval reached 0.8 drinks (10 g each) a day and which moved to about half a drink a day when the same group updated its weights (0.534, 0–1.00; Bryazka et al., 2022); the 2016 authors expect their figures to be underestimates, because drinking patterns, harm to others from violence and people under 15 were left out; and the two estimates used different methods and inputs, so the difference between them is not a trend. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated by the same team.
claims.magnitude: Griswold et al. 2018 (GBD 2016; 95% uncertainty intervals): 2.8 million (2.4–3.3) deaths in 2016; 2.2% (1.5–3.0) of age-standardised female and 6.8% (5.8–8.0) of male deaths; 1.6% (1.4–2.0) and 6.0% (5.4–6.7) of DALYs; ages 15–49: 3.8% (3.2–4.3) of female and 12.2% (10.8–13.6) of male deaths; leading attributable causes at 15–49: tuberculosis 1.4% (1.0–1.7), road injuries 1.2% (0.7–1.9) and self-harm 1.1% (0.6–1.5) of total deaths; minimum-risk level 0 (0.0–0.8) standard drinks of 10 g a day. Rehm et al. 2009 (WHO comparative risk assessment, 2004; thousands; no intervals): caused 2482 (men 2039, women 443); prevented 227 (cardiovascular 215, diabetes 12); net 2255 (men 1944, women 311) of 58 738 deaths, 3.8% (men 6.3%, women 1.1%); under age 60, 5.3% (men 7.9%, women 1.9%); deaths caused by cause: unintentional injuries 666, cardiovascular 545, cancer 487, cirrhosis 373, intentional injuries 272, neuropsychiatric 135, perinatal 3. Bryazka et al. 2022: global minimum-risk level 0.534 (0–1.00) drinks a day with the GBD 2016 curves and GBD 2020 weights.

claims.statement: In adults followed in prospective cohort studies of drinking and death (published 1981 to 2021, mostly from North America, Europe and Australia), drinking a little (about 1.3 to 25 g of ethanol a day, from one 10-g drink a week to about two drinks a day) compared with not drinking: the evidence is insufficient to say whether it changes the risk of dying from any cause, and the question is disputed. Against non-drinkers as each study defined them, who in most studies included people who had stopped drinking or drank occasionally, people who drank a little died at lower rates: in a 2006 pooled analysis of 34 cohorts (1,015,835 people, 94,533 deaths) the death rate was lowest at 6 g a day, about half a drink (relative risk 0.81, 95% CI 0.80 to 0.83), and stayed lower up to 42 g a day; in 87 and then 107 cohorts (up to 4,838,825 people and 425,564 deaths) the relative risk at 1.3 to 25 g a day was 0.86 (0.83 to 0.90, and 0.83 to 0.88). These analyses give relative risks only, so the difference cannot be given as a number out of 100 (editors' observation). The difference shrinks or disappears as the comparison group is defined more strictly: people who had stopped drinking, some of them because of illness, died at higher rates than abstainers in the main models (relative risks 1.22 to 1.38); against occasional drinkers, people who drank a little had no lower death rate (1.02, 0.95 to 1.10; 0.97, 0.85 to 1.11 after adjustment), while abstainers had a higher one with limited adjustment (1.19, 1.12 to 1.27) but not after adjustment (1.04, 0.94 to 1.16); after adjustment for study characteristics, including how each study defined its non-drinkers, the estimate was 0.97 (0.88 to 1.07) in 87 cohorts and 0.93 (0.85 to 1.01) in 107; in the 13 cohorts that compared with people who had never drunk it was 0.90 (0.76 to 1.06); and in the 6 cohorts that did so and had recruited people at a median age of 55 or younger, 0.98 (0.87 to 1.11), against 0.84 (0.79 to 0.89) in 18 older cohorts whose non-drinkers included former and occasional drinkers. Even in 2006, cohorts whose comparison group left out former and light drinkers showed a smaller reduction (16% against 23% at the lowest point) that ended at 30 rather than 52 g a day. The 2016, 2023 and 2024 analyses are by one research group and reuse the same cohorts; the 6-cohort estimate rests on studies the article does not name and allows anything from a 13% lower to an 11% higher death rate (editors' arithmetic); and genetic studies, which avoid the non-drinker comparison, concern heart disease and diabetes rather than deaths from all causes (see the answers on the heart). None of these designs can show whether drinking a little itself makes people live longer or shorter. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
claims.magnitude: Di Castelnuovo et al. 2006 (34 cohorts, 56 curves, 1,015,835 people, 94,533 deaths; fixed-effect; against each study's lowest-intake category): lowest relative risk 0.81 (95% CI 0.80 to 0.83) at 6 g a day, lower mortality significant up to 42 g a day; adjusted at least for age 17% lower (99% CI 15% to 18%) at 6 g, up to 37 g; with light or former drinkers in the reference group 23% (20% to 26%) at 8 g, up to 52 g; without them 16% (14% to 18%) at 5 g, up to 30 g; the same 34 curves 19% (17% to 21%) crude and 16% (14% to 18%) adjusted. Stockwell et al. 2016 (87 cohorts, 3,998,626 people, 367,103 deaths), low volume 1.30 to 24.9 g a day: against study-defined abstainers 0.86 (0.83 to 0.90), occasional 0.84 (0.79 to 0.89), former 1.22 (1.14 to 1.31); against occasional drinkers, low volume 1.02 (0.95 to 1.10), abstainers 1.19 (1.12 to 1.27); with all study-level covariates, low volume 0.97 (0.88 to 1.07), former 1.38 (1.24 to 1.54); six covariates 0.89 (0.84 to 0.94); 13 lifetime-abstainer studies 0.90 (0.76 to 1.06), former 1.31 (1.09 to 1.57); 7 higher-quality studies 0.89 (0.62 to 1.29), 1.04 (0.95 to 1.15) without one influential study. Zhao et al. 2023 (107 cohorts, 4,838,825 people, 425,564 deaths): unadjusted low volume 0.85 (0.81 to 0.88); fully adjusted 0.93 (0.85 to 1.01; P = .07), occasional 0.96 (0.86 to 1.06), former 1.26 (1.12 to 1.42); against occasional drinkers, fully adjusted, low volume 0.97 (0.85 to 1.11), abstainers 1.04 (0.94 to 1.16); I2 above 85.87% in every category. Stockwell et al. 2024 (subgroups of the 107; random study effect): all 107, 0.86 (0.83 to 0.88; 99 studies with low-volume estimates); 6 studies of cohorts recruited at a median age of 55 or younger against lifetime abstainers 0.98 (0.87 to 1.11), 1.10 (0.97 to 1.24) without the random effect; with a 30-day intake measure as well, 5 studies, 1.04 (0.95 to 1.15); older cohorts with both abstainer biases, 18 studies, 0.84 (0.79 to 0.89); one criterion only, 0.88 (0.84 to 0.92; 51 studies) and 0.88 (0.81 to 0.95; 18 studies); editors' calculation of the difference between 0.98 and 0.84, treating the two sets of studies as independent: ratio 1.17 (95% CI 1.02 to 1.34), p of about .03. No absolute death rates by drinking group in any of the four.

claims.statement: In the world's population aged 15 and older, as modelled in two Global Burden of Disease (GBD) analyses, the second an update of the first that keeps 17 of its curves, drinking compared with not drinking is associated with a combined risk of 22 or 23 alcohol-linked diseases and injuries (each weighted by its share of the population's ill health, measured in disability-adjusted life years, DALYs) that is lowest at or near zero for people aged 15 to 39, and at about half a standard drink (10 g of ethanol) a day for people aged 40 and older: these are model estimates resting on relative-risk curves fitted to observational studies of self-reported drinking, and every lowest point above zero comes from lower risks of ischaemic heart disease, ischaemic stroke and diabetes in those studies (editors' reading of how the models are built), which genetic studies mostly do not find. In GBD 2016 (Griswold et al., 2018), one curve weighted by the world's 2016 disease mix had its lowest point at 0 standard drinks a day (95% uncertainty interval 0 to 0.8 a day; the abstract prints it per week) and rose with intake; of its 23 conditions only ischaemic heart disease had a significant dip (lowest relative risk 0.86 in men at 0.83 drinks a day and 0.82 in women at 0.92), diabetes and ischaemic stroke dipped non-significantly, and the risks of all the others, every cancer among them, rose with intake; in women the lower heart disease and diabetes risks were offset mainly by cancers. In GBD 2020 (Bryazka et al., 2022), with weights from each region's, age group's and sex's own disease mix, the lowest point at ages 15 to 39 was 0 to 0.603 drinks a day across regions (worldwide 0.136 for men and 0.273 for women), and the combined risk was back at a non-drinker's level at 0.249 drinks a day for men and 0.546 for women worldwide (about 2.5 and 5.5 g; editors' arithmetic), injuries, whose risk rose with intake, making up much of the ill health weighed at these ages (66.3% in men, 47.9% in women); at 40 to 64 the lowest point was 0.527 (men) and 0.562 (women) drinks a day and the non-drinker level was reached at 1.69 and 1.82; at 65 and older, 0.636 and 0.656, and 3.19 and 3.51. Differences between women and men were not significant. Worldwide and age-standardised, the 2020 lowest point was 0.511 (0.400 to 0.700) drinks a day, and 0.534 (0 to 1.00) when the 2016 curves were given the 2020 weights, so the move away from zero comes mostly from the weights (editors' reading). The lowest-risk amount is the bottom of an average of many curves for a whole population, not one person's risk and not a risk-free amount; drinking a lot on some days was not modelled, alcohol use disorder, depression, anxiety and dementia were left out of the 2020 curves, and the authors expect that including the last three would lower the amounts. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
claims.magnitude: GBD 2016 (Griswold et al., 2018; 23 outcomes, 592 studies, 3,992 relative-risk estimates; one curve weighted by global age-standardised 2016 DALY rates, both sexes; standard drink 10 g): lowest point of the weighted curve 0 standard drinks a day (95% UI 0.0 to 0.8 a day; printed per week in the abstract), rising monotonically; ischaemic heart disease lowest relative risk 0.86 (0.80 to 0.96) in men at 0.83 drinks a day and 0.82 (0.72 to 0.95) in women at 0.92; non-significant dips for diabetes and ischaemic stroke; all cancers rising. GBD 2020 (Bryazka et al., 2022; 22 curves, five re-fitted with 71 more studies; weights by region, age, sex and year; TMREL the lowest point, NDE the return to a non-drinker's risk; standard drinks a day): all populations, TMREL 0 (0 to 0) to 1.87 (0.500 to 3.30); ages 15 to 39 across regions TMREL 0 to 0.603 (0.400 to 1.00), NDE 0.002 (0 to 0) to 1.75 (0.698 to 4.30); global males TMREL 0.136 (0 to 0.400), NDE 0.249 (0 to 1.00), females 0.273 (0 to 0.500) and 0.546 (0 to 1.30); ages 40 to 64, males 0.527 (0.400 to 1.00) and 1.69 (0.800 to 3.20), females 0.562 (0.400 to 0.800) and 1.82 (1.00 to 3.10); 65 and older, males 0.636 (0.500 to 1.00) and 3.19 (1.50 to 5.20), females 0.656 (0.500 to 1.00) and 3.51 (1.70 to 5.50); ages 40 and older across regions, TMREL 0.114 (0 to 0.403) to 1.87 (0.500 to 3.30), NDE 0.193 (0 to 0.900) to 6.94 (3.40 to 8.30). Global, age-standardised, both sexes: GBD 2016 0 (0 to 0.800); GBD 2016 curves with 2020 weights 0.534 (0 to 1.00), NDE 0.669 (0 to 1.40); GBD 2020 0.511 (0.400 to 0.700), NDE 1.72 (0.80 to 3.30). Hypothetical curves for alcohol use disorders and alcoholic cardiomyopathy lowered the TMREL by 0.058 to 0.146 drinks a day on average. In grams (editors' arithmetic, 10 g a drink): 0.249 drinks is about 2.5 g, 0.546 about 5.5 g, 0.511 about 5.1 g.
